Issued at 132 PM CDT Fri Aug 21 2026

Early this afternoon, a decaying MCS is pushing south across 
far northern IL along an north-south oriented instability 
gradient draped very roughly along the I-39 corridor. 
Additionally, scattered showers are moving east near and north 
of the Kankakee River valley as a subtle leading shortwave works
across. This MCS has been on a very gradual weakening trend, 
but it managed to hold together much better than any recent 
guidance had thought. It's still generating a fair amount of 
lightning and pockets of heavier rainfall near its leading edge 
which will likely persist as it continues to drop south across 
the Chicago metro through the afternoon. No strong or severe 
storms are expected through mid-afternoon with this system, but 
embedded downpours will likely remain. 

Farther upstream, a more potent shortwave trough axis is 
swinging into the upper Midwest coincident with a surface cold 
front stretching from western WI southwest into northeast and 
central IA. It's along and ahead of the front this evening where
we expect a chance for severe convection. The first showers 
have just started to go up along the front near La Crosse. 
Thunderstorms are expected to blossom along the boundary as it 
continues southeastward and eventually crosses into northern IL 
near the end of the afternoon. SPC mesoanalysis suggests 
instability is building quickly west of I- 39 in a region of 
efficient theta-e advection ahead of the front. CAM guidance has
been rather consistent on a tongue of 2,500 to 3,000 Joules of 
MLCAPE building into our western and northwestern CWA by late 
afternoon. It's not clear the quality of the thermo environment 
farther east this evening between this MCS, added daytime cloud 
cover, and eventually diurnal cooling into the evening. All 
along, guidance had been resolving notably less instability with
eastward extent largely owing to a drier low level airmass and 
diurnal cooling through the evening. However, the added rain and
cloud cover could be enough to greatly inhibit much of a severe
threat east of the Fox Valley and especially into northwest 
Indiana, but there's not great confidence there.

Effective shear this evening is marginal to fair at about 25 to
35 kt, highest in our west. However, models do resolve a 
veering low level shear profile which would support a low-end 
tornado threat where the low levels can destabilize 
sufficiently. Even when discounting this ongoing MCS, CAMs had 
been consistently hanging onto some low level capping roughly 
east of the Fox Valley through the afternoon, and would imagine 
that's even more likely now, before being further reinforced by 
diurnal cooling. For that reason, this evening's marginal 
tornado threat will be focused west of the Fox Valley and north 
of I-80 where the more supportive low level thermo environment 
is anticipated. This is also where the severe wind and hail 
threat will be maximized given the greater instability and 
generally more support expected from the left exit region of a 
700 mb jet max out to our west. Severe hail and damaging winds 
are on the table area-wide but it's not clear the 
eastward/southeastward extent of deep convection this evening 
and it's very possible much of the area is spared from severe 
weather.

Areas of very heavy rainfall are expected as well, in addition 
to the ongoing pockets of heavy rain within the remnant MCS. 
The storms look progressive enough in nature to avoid many 
widespread flooding concerns, but scattered pockets of 1-2" with
the evening coverage alone is a strongly favored signal among 
guidance which would likely lead to localized flooding impacts, 
mainly in low-lying and other flood prone areas. The severe 
threat looks to exit the area to the southeast shortly after 
midnight.

The upper trough will continue digging into the Great Lakes 
region through tomorrow and drive a vort max across WI and Lake 
Michigan during the day tomorrow. Isolated to widely scattered 
showers and storms will attempt to develop on the back side of 
the system and fall on parts of the area tomorrow afternoon. 
With the cooler mid level air spilling over, as many as 1,500 to
2,000 Joules of MUCAPE is favored to develop over NE IL and NW 
IN for the afternoon. Nothing too strong or severe is 
anticipated, but if one or two more robust updrafts can develop 
and survive through significant dry air aloft, it may be enough
to spit out some locally heavy rain and gusty thunderstorm 
winds. Most of the area will be staying dry tomorrow with highs 
forecast in the upper 70s to around 80.

Strong northerly winds will develop on Lake Michigan tomorrow 
and generate high waves and dangerous currents at northwest 
Indiana beaches leading to hazardous swimming conditions. Such
